findings.where: Hero, desktop: the handwritten 'write to me' note in the left margin, beside the italic experience line
findings.fault: The page's only call to action sits in the narrow margin, outside the column where the name, offer and credential are read. It is set apart from them and looks like a scribbled annotation rather than the way to get in touch. A visitor reading heading → subline → photo can finish the first screen without seeing it.
findings.who_objects: A development-bank staffer who has read the credential and wants to contact Mark has to hunt for how to do it. The one action the homepage exists for is the easiest part of the screen to pass over.

findings.where: Hero 'write to me' link (both widths), and the article specimen, which ends with no contact line or footer
findings.fault: The only contact route is a bare mailto behind 'write to me'. Mark's email address appears nowhere as visible text, and the tile shows no footer that carries it, although the palette assigns a footer colour. A visitor without a desktop mail client gets nothing when they click, and cannot copy the address.
findings.who_objects: An agency staffer on webmail or a locked-down work machine, or one who wants to forward Mark's address to a procurement colleague, finds no address to copy. An article reader who arrives from a LinkedIn post has no visible way to reach Mark.

findings.where: Hero, the italic line 'Over 40 years of international infrastructure experience.'
findings.fault: The credibility line is a size word ('40 years'), not checkable work. The brief asks for one strong line and no boasts. The line sits directly under the far stronger and more specific World Bank credential, and it weakens it into a generic consultancy claim.
findings.who_objects: A bank or agency reader who selects consultants against terms of reference trusts named roles, bodies and regions, and discounts year counts as brochure talk. Mark asked for a personal advisor's voice, not a firm's.

findings.where: Hero, the name heading and subline (first screen, both widths)
findings.fault: The first screen says what Mark does but not where he works: it gives no base country and no regions. Who the advice is for is left to the reader to infer from the World Bank credential. 'International' is all the 5-second test gets on where.
findings.who_objects: A staffer at a regional development bank who needs someone with experience in their region cannot tell from the first screen whether Mark has it, and that is the first thing they must be sure of before writing.

findings.where: Whole page, the first screen and below
findings.fault: The page carries no proof beyond the one self-stated credential. It has no selected work, no named bodies that asked for the work, and no links to work hosted by those bodies. The lecture row, the only outside evidence, gives no venue.
findings.who_objects: A first-time visitor from a development agency has nothing they can check before getting in touch. The lecture without its host (who invited Mark, and where) loses most of its value as standing.

findings.where: Article specimen, the pull quote 'Whichever PPP Law I am currently working on with a client country!' set large in the handwriting face
findings.fault: The article's punchline is set big in a casual felt-pen script. That breaks the tile's own rule of one handwritten note per view, which is the call to action in the margin and never body text. A wry aside becomes the loudest thing on the article page and reads as flippant.
findings.who_objects: A bank reader who opened the article to judge Mark's thinking on PPP law gets a joke in comic-style lettering as its centrepiece, which undercuts the experienced lawyer the article is meant to show. Angélique, adding posts, also has no clear rule for when the hand is allowed.
